name: Cyrillic (Russian)
signature: Latin-like at a glance, but studded with give-aways: Я, Ж, Д, Б, и.
combination: A true alphabet: letters are written left-to-right in a row and each spells a sound. No inherent vowels, no diacritics in normal text (stress is unmarked). Two letters — ъ (hard sign) and ь (soft sign) — spell no sound of their own; they modify the consonant before them.
notes: The 33 lowercase Russian letters. complete:false because the UPPERCASE forms are not yet in the inventory (lessons use the lowercase citation form); the lowercase set itself is whole. Several letters are 'false friends' that look like Latin letters but sound different — those are flagged. Descended from Greek (via Old Church Slavonic), so many letters are Greek cousins: С↔sigma, Р↔rho, П↔pi, Ф↔phi.

In the 07:50–07:55 lowercase у demonstration, the pen begins at the upper left, descends to the baseline, turns upward without lifting through the right arm, retraces down through that arm into a long descender, curls left around a lower loop, crosses the descender, and rises into a short rightward exit in one continuous pen-down run, for zero intervening lifts. The demonstrated school hand resembles a loop-descender Latin y with a narrow rounded upper body and rising exit; the bundled Noto Sans Cyrillic glyph is a printed y-like form with two straight upper arms and a broad descender that curves left without a loop or exit join. This learner path preserves the source's left-arm-to-right-arm-to-descender order and zero-lift evidence while fitting the printed outline: descend the left arm, rise through the right arm, retrace to the junction, continue through the long descender, and curve left through its terminal without lifting. Connected cursive restores the source's lower loop and rising exit, and individual handwriting may round, narrow, widen, or slant the upper body and descender differently.

strokeOrderSource.citation: RussianIrina, ‘Learning Russian - Alphabet letters, handwriting’, lowercase ф demonstration, 08:16–08:26, YouTube, 5 February 2013
strokeOrderSource.variation: The native-teacher video presents all 33 Russian letters first in print and then in the classic handwritten form taught at school. In the 08:16–08:26 lowercase ф demonstration, the pen first descends the long central stem from the upper line below the baseline, lifts once, restarts near the upper central junction, circles a narrow left loop, crosses the stem, circles a narrow right loop, and finishes through a small rising exit. The demonstrated school hand therefore uses two pen-down runs with one intervening lift: stem first, then the linked left-to-right looped body. The bundled Noto Sans Cyrillic glyph is a printed phi-like form with one straight central ascender-descender and two wider upright bowls without an exit join. This learner path preserves the source's stem-before-left-loop-before-right-loop order and one-lift evidence while fitting the printed outline: descend the central stem, lift, trace the left bowl, cross through the central junction, and trace the right bowl. Connected cursive restores the source's narrower linked loops and rising exit, and individual handwriting may round, narrow, widen, or slant the bowls and stem differently.
